title: President Trump says Irish reunification ‘would be a fantastic thing,’ during visit to Ireland | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump said Saturday that Irish reunification “would be a fantastic thing” during a bilateral meeting with Ireland’s Taoiseach Micheál Martin, something he projected “would happen eventually.”

When a reporter asked his view on reunification of Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, and the Republic of Ireland, Trump at first acknowledged his comments could inflame a politically sensitive issue before voicing support.

“Well, I don’t want to cause any trouble,” Trump said. “But I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” arguing it would be “a great feather in everybody’s cap.”

Trump also suggested that reunification would happen eventually and questioned how it could be a negative thing.

“It’s going to happen eventually. You know what? It’s going to happen eventually. I think it will happen now. You’ve got the right man over here to get it moving,” Trump said, pointing at Martin. “But yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the UK will have something to say about obviously, but I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”

Trump touched down in Ireland Saturday morning, to hold talks with the country’s leaders before attending a tournament at one of his golf courses.

Trump, wearing a red tie, was greeted on the tarmac by several dignitaries including Ireland’s finance minister Simon Harris, foreign minister Helen McEntee, US Ambassador to Ireland Edward Walsh and Irish Ambassador to the US Geraldine Byrne Nason.

Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, disembarked from the plane afterward and also greeted officials on the ground.

Trump briefly answered a couple questions on his way back into the Beast after the courtesy call with Irish President Catherine Connolly, including one concerning trafficthrough the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

“Everything will work out just fine. It’s all going to work out fine,” Trump said.

Connolly did not engage with press who shouted questions, instead staring ahead from the residence as Trump left the premises.

The last time Trump visited Ireland as president was during his first term in June 2019. This visit takes Trump out the US at a crucial time for him politically, just weeks before the midterms and as the Iran-backed Houthis’ rapid advance in Yemen threatens to open a second front in the war with Iran.

During his time in Ireland, Trump will largely be shielded from the public and kept away from expected protests. Instead, he will be ferried by motorcade straight to three official government residences in Phoenix Park, a huge urban park in central Dublin which officials have closed since Friday night.

There, he will hold a bilateral meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and deliver remarks to business leaders at US Ambassador to Ireland Edward Walsh’s residence, a White House official told CNN.

The president’s meetings with Irish political leaders will touch on bilateral economic cooperation, creating business opportunities for US industry, and discussing international issues of mutual interest, the official said.

Trump’s visit presents a tricky balancing act for the Irish government. On the one hand, US companies, many of whom have their European headquarters in Ireland, are hugely important for the country’s economy while, on the other, Trump remains unpopular with much of the Irish public and some protests are expected.

Alongside a demonstration planned for Saturday afternoon in central Dublin, protests are also expected to take place in Doonbeg, the village in the west of Ireland where Trump’s golf course is located and also at Shannon Airport.

Shannon Airport has served as a key gateway for the US military for decades, used as a refueling stop for US troops traveling to Afghanistan and Iraq. Numerous protests have been held by anti-war activist groups at the airport over the years protesting the US military’s use of the facility.

Back in 1984, then-President Ronald Reagan’s visit to Ireland was marked by protests. Archival footage fromRTÉ Newsshows thousands participating in a “ring around Reagan” protest, including anti-nuclear groups. “REFUSE CRUISE” was written on makeshift missiles and video shows a banner with “$ FOR WANT NOT FOR WAR” written on it.

After wrapping up his meetings in Dublin, Trump will head west on Sunday to his Doonbeg course where he will attend the Irish Open tournament.

His son, Eric, told Irish national broadcaster RTÉ that the golf course is the largest employer in the local area.

“Go down to Morrissey’s tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family,” he said. “Go have them attest to what we’ve done for the country and what we’ve invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them.”

Connolly was among those who protested Trump’s visit in 2019 before she was elected to the ceremonial position of Ireland’s president in 2025. Hosting Martin in the Oval Office for a visit on St. Patrick’s Day in March, Trump referred to Connolly as a “he” when asked by an Irish reporter about hercommentsabout “violations of international law” in the Middle East.

“Look, he’s lucky I exist, that’s all I can say,” Trump said. “If you’re gonna allow countries that are sick and demented – and they are demented – to have nuclear weapons–everybody in the whole world should be very thankful.”

Dressed in a black suit, Connolly greeted Trump at Áras an Uachtaráin, shook hands and briefly exchanged words before heading inside where Trump signed the guest book. They emerged to watch a band play the American and Irish national anthems.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

CNN’s Niamh Kennedy contributed reporting.

CNN’s Niamh Kennedy contributed reporting.
